quests.question: When the auditor asked one simple question about company accounts, it uncovered dozens of unresolved financial issues. Which idiom describes what that question did?
quests.hint: Imagine a small metal can that, once opened, releases far more mess than you expected.
quests.explanation: 'Open a can of worms' means to start a process or raise a topic that leads to many complicated, unexpected problems. Example: 'Changing that policy will open a can of worms — too many people disagree.' It suggests unleashing a messy, complex situation.
quests.usageContext: Common when a small action unexpectedly reveals a much bigger, messier problem.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: No one had any warning when the company announced it was closing immediately — it came as a total shock to everyone. Which idiom describes how the news arrived?
quests.hint: Picture something falling from a clear, empty sky with no warning at all.
quests.explanation: 'Out of the blue' means something that happens suddenly and unexpectedly, with no prior warning. Example: 'He called me out of the blue after five years of silence.' It comes from the image of lightning striking from a clear blue sky.
quests.usageContext: Common in both casual and news contexts to describe sudden, unpredicted events.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: For a simple birthday dinner, the host arranged one hundred balloons, a live band, a fireworks display, and a five-course meal — far beyond anything anyone expected. Which idiom describes the celebration?
quests.hint: This is about going far beyond what any reasonable occasion would call for.
quests.explanation: 'Over the top' means excessive, exaggerated, or going far beyond what is considered appropriate or reasonable. Example: 'His reaction to losing the game was completely over the top.' It is often abbreviated as OTT in informal speech.
quests.usageContext: Often mildly critical or amused in tone; common when describing extravagant behaviour.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: When the customer complained about a billing error, each department told him to speak to another department, and no one accepted responsibility for fixing it. Which idiom describes the employees' behaviour?
quests.hint: Picture responsibility being handed off like a small object nobody wants to keep.
quests.explanation: 'Pass the buck' means to shift responsibility or blame to someone else instead of dealing with it yourself. Example: 'Don't pass the buck — this was your mistake and you need to fix it.' It originates from poker, where a marker was passed to indicate whose turn it was to deal.
quests.usageContext: Critical in tone; common in workplace contexts describing avoidance of accountability.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Although the job required several years of experience, the candidate secured it because his uncle was the CEO. Which idiom describes how he obtained the position?
quests.hint: Think of someone controlling events from behind the scenes, like a puppeteer.
quests.explanation: 'Pull strings' means to use personal connections or influence to get something done, often in an unfair or unofficial way. Example: 'She pulled strings to get her son into the exclusive school.' It comes from the image of a puppeteer controlling a puppet with hidden strings.
quests.usageContext: Often slightly disapproving; suggests an unfair advantage through personal connections rather than ability.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: The investor put every penny he owned into one company's stock. When that company failed, he lost absolutely everything. Which idiom warns against this behaviour?
quests.hint: If you drop the one basket holding everything, you lose it all at once.
quests.explanation: 'Put all your eggs in one basket' means to risk everything on a single option or outcome. Example: 'Don't put all your eggs in one basket — apply to several universities.' It refers to the danger of carrying all your eggs in one container, risking total loss.
options: put all your eggs in one basket
quests.usageContext: Common as a warning in financial or planning contexts, urging caution against over-reliance on one option.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: At dinner, Mike mentioned how much he hated a particular restaurant, unaware that the owner was sitting right next to him. Which idiom describes Mike's social blunder?
quests.hint: Imagine the physical awkwardness of literally putting your own foot in your mouth.
quests.explanation: 'Put your foot in your mouth' means to say something embarrassing or socially awkward without realising it. Example: 'I really put my foot in my mouth when I asked if she was pregnant — she wasn't.' It suggests an unintentional conversational blunder.
options: put his foot in his mouth
quests.usageContext: Common and often used humorously about an accidental, embarrassing comment.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Even though several employees disagreed with the new management policy, nobody wanted to speak up and risk causing conflict or disruption within the team. Nobody wanted to do what?
quests.hint: Everyone else wants the boat to stay steady - this is about disturbing that balance.
quests.explanation: 'Rock the boat' means to do or say something that disturbs a stable situation or creates unwanted conflict. Example: 'Everyone seemed happy with the arrangement, so I didn't want to rock the boat by suggesting changes.' It suggests avoiding disruption.
quests.usageContext: Common when discussing reluctance to challenge the status quo, especially in groups or teams.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: The team held four separate meetings about the new product launch but failed to reach any decisions or make any real progress each time. Which idiom describes their efforts?
quests.hint: Picture a lot of movement and effort that always ends up back where it started.
quests.explanation: 'Run around in circles' means to waste time doing activities that produce no useful result. Example: 'We've been running around in circles on this issue — we need a completely different approach.' It suggests frustrating, unproductive effort.
quests.usageContext: Common in frustrated descriptions of meetings or projects that go nowhere despite effort.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Six months before the company went bankrupt, its best employees had already started resigning, one by one. Those who left early had read the warning signs clearly. Which idiom describes their awareness?
quests.hint: This comes from an ancient story about a mysterious warning appearing on a wall before disaster struck.
quests.explanation: 'See the writing on the wall' means to recognise early signs that something bad is going to happen. Example: 'She saw the writing on the wall and resigned before the company collapsed.' It comes from the biblical story of Belshazzar's Feast.
options: saw the writing on the wall
quests.usageContext: Common when praising or noting someone's foresight in recognising an approaching change.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: After work, the coworkers sat outside in the sunshine and chatted casually about their weekends, sport, and nothing in particular. Which idiom describes what they were doing?
quests.hint: This is about relaxed, aimless conversation, not a focused discussion with a goal.
quests.explanation: 'Shoot the breeze' means to have a casual, relaxed conversation about unimportant topics. Example: 'We stayed after the meeting, just shooting the breeze for a while.' It suggests friendly, informal conversation with no specific purpose.
quests.usageContext: Very casual; describes friendly small talk rather than any serious or work-related exchange.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: When her colleague offered to handle all the paperwork 'just to help,' Laura felt uneasy — something about his offer seemed dishonest. Which idiom describes her instinct?
quests.hint: Long before you see anything wrong, a bad smell can already warn you something's off.
quests.explanation: 'Smell a rat' means to become suspicious that something dishonest or wrong is happening. Example: 'When the salesman avoided my questions, I started to smell a rat.' It comes from the idea of detecting a hidden rodent by its scent before you can see it.
options: gave him the benefit of the doubt
quests.usageContext: Common when describing suspicion based on instinct rather than solid proof.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: At a formal black-tie event, one guest arrived in a bright orange tracksuit. Every eye in the room turned to stare at him. Which idiom describes the guest?
quests.hint: A thumb, if injured, is impossible not to notice among the other fingers.
quests.explanation: 'Stick out like a sore thumb' means to be very obviously different from everyone or everything around you. Example: 'The bright pink house sticks out like a sore thumb on the row of grey buildings.' A sore thumb naturally draws attention wherever it goes.
options: stuck out like a sore thumb
quests.usageContext: Common and often visual, describing something or someone clearly out of place in their surroundings.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Carlos loved posting controversial opinions online and starting rumours at the office just to see how colleagues would react. Which idiom describes his behaviour?
quests.hint: Think of someone stirring a calm pot just to watch it bubble over.
quests.explanation: 'Stir the pot' means to deliberately cause trouble or conflict, usually by raising controversial topics or spreading rumours. Example: 'She's always stirring the pot by gossiping about colleagues.' It comes from the image of stirring a cooking pot and making it boil over.
quests.usageContext: Critical in tone; describes someone who enjoys provoking conflict, often for entertainment.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: For months, the record label kept telling the young artist they were 'almost ready to sign her' — but they had no real intention of ever doing so. Which idiom describes what they were doing?
quests.hint: Picture leading someone forward on a leash, always promising the destination is close.
quests.explanation: 'String someone along' means to keep someone waiting or hoping with false promises, deliberately deceiving them. Example: 'He strung her along for two years with promises of commitment he never intended to keep.' It suggests dishonest delay.
quests.usageContext: Often used about romantic relationships or professional promises that are never actually fulfilled.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: A friend claims the new café is 'the absolute best in the entire city,' but you know she tends to exaggerate everything. How should you treat her recommendation?
quests.hint: A small pinch of salt makes something easier to swallow without fully trusting it.
quests.explanation: 'Take something with a grain of salt' means to not completely believe something because you suspect it may be exaggerated or inaccurate. Example: 'His reviews of his own cooking should be taken with a grain of salt.' It comes from the ancient practice of adding salt to make things easier to swallow.
options: take it with a grain of salt
quests.usageContext: Common advice when a source of information is known to exaggerate or be unreliable.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: After weeks of small issues with a noisy neighbour, the moment the music started again at 2 AM was the moment Sarah finally called the police. Which idiom describes that final incident?
quests.hint: Picture a heavy load that one small extra piece finally makes impossible to carry.
quests.explanation: 'The last straw' (from 'the straw that broke the camel's back') means the final problem in a series that causes someone to finally react or lose patience. Example: 'His constant lateness was bad enough, but arriving late to a client meeting was the last straw.' It comes from the image of adding weight until it becomes too much.
quests.usageContext: Common when describing the tipping point after a long period of frustration.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Before handing over the project to her successor, the manager spent her last week ensuring every remaining small task was completed and nothing was left unfinished. Which idiom describes what she was doing?
quests.hint: Picture a few loose threads that need a final knot before something is truly finished.
quests.explanation: 'Tie up loose ends' means to complete remaining small tasks or details before finishing something. Example: 'Before I go on holiday, I need to tie up a few loose ends at the office.' It comes from the image of knotting thread ends to prevent unravelling.
options: going back to the drawing board
quests.usageContext: Common in professional handovers, describing careful, thorough completion before moving on.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Despite all his efforts to save the struggling business over two years, James finally accepted that it was impossible and decided to stop. Which idiom describes his decision?
quests.hint: This comes from boxing, where a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight.
quests.explanation: 'Throw in the towel' means to give up or admit defeat. Example: 'After years of trying to get a record deal, she finally threw in the towel and pursued a different career.' It comes from boxing, where trainers throw a towel into the ring to stop a fight.
quests.usageContext: Common when describing someone quitting after trying hard, often with some sympathy rather than blame.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: The company hasn't decided whether to open a new office yet — senior management is still debating both sides of the argument. Which idiom describes the state of the decision?
quests.hint: Nothing has landed yet - the decision is still floating, unsettled.
quests.explanation: 'Up in the air' means uncertain, not yet decided. Example: 'Our holiday plans are still up in the air — we haven't bought tickets yet.' It suggests something floating without direction, like plans not yet grounded in reality.
quests.usageContext: Common in planning contexts to describe details that haven't been confirmed yet.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: After her husband had a sharp outburst the previous day, Carla was extremely careful about every word she said to avoid upsetting him again. Which idiom describes how she was behaving?
quests.hint: Imagine trying to walk across a floor covered in eggshells without cracking a single one.
quests.explanation: 'Walk on eggshells' means to be very careful about what you say or do in order to avoid upsetting someone. Example: 'Ever since the argument, I've been walking on eggshells around him.' It comes from the image of treading gently to avoid cracking fragile eggs.
options: put her foot in her mouth
quests.usageContext: Common when describing tense relationships where one person fears upsetting the other.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Everyone around Lucas always knew exactly how he was feeling — whether happy, upset, or angry — because he never hid his emotions at all. Which idiom describes Lucas?
quests.hint: Picture emotions visible right there on a sleeve, impossible to hide.
quests.explanation: 'Wear your heart on your sleeve' means to show your feelings openly without trying to hide them. Example: 'She wears her heart on her sleeve, so you always know when she's upset.' It comes from a medieval tradition of knights wearing a lady's token on their sleeve.
options: wore his heart on his sleeve
played his cards close to his chest
quests.usageContext: Common when describing someone who is emotionally open and easy to read.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: A sceptical friend, asked if she would ever enjoy extreme sports, responded that it would essentially never happen in her lifetime. Which idiom might she have used?
quests.hint: This names something physically impossible to make a point about how unlikely an event is.
quests.explanation: 'When pigs fly' means something will never happen. Example: 'He'll clean his room when pigs fly!' It uses the image of something impossible — pigs flying — to emphasise that an event is extremely unlikely or will simply never occur.
quests.usageContext: Humorous and informal; a sarcastic way of saying something is extremely unlikely.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Ana passed all five of her final university exams with excellent grades, making her family enormously proud. Which idiom describes her outstanding success?
quests.hint: Picture a ship sailing home with all its flags proudly raised, signalling total triumph.
quests.explanation: 'With flying colors' means to pass or complete something with great success and high marks. Example: 'He completed the certification programme with flying colors.' It originally referred to a victorious ship sailing with its flags — its 'colors' — proudly flying.
options: by the skin of her teeth
quests.usageContext: Positive and celebratory; common when praising outstanding results, especially in exams or tests.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: The charming and friendly investment adviser turned out to be running a massive fraud scheme that had cheated hundreds of clients out of their savings. Which idiom describes him?
quests.hint: Underneath a harmless, friendly disguise hides something far more dangerous.
quests.explanation: 'A wolf in sheep's clothing' means someone who appears harmless or friendly but is actually dangerous or dishonest. Example: 'The trustworthy-seeming broker was a wolf in sheep's clothing.' It comes from a biblical phrase about hidden danger disguised as something safe.
quests.usageContext: Common when warning about someone whose true, harmful intentions are hidden behind charm.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: The nurse worked 16-hour shifts, seven days a week, for three straight months during the health crisis, giving everything she had. Which idiom describes her dedication?
quests.hint: This describes effort so intense it feels like it could wear your body down to nothing.
quests.explanation: 'Work your fingers to the bone' means to work extremely hard for an extended period of time. Example: 'My grandmother worked her fingers to the bone to give her children a better life.' It emphasises physical and emotional exhaustion from relentless overwork.
options: worked her fingers to the bone
quests.usageContext: Sympathetic and admiring in tone; common when praising someone's exhausting dedication.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Tom wanted to quit his job and travel the world, but also wanted to keep earning his full salary. His friend pointed out the obvious contradiction. Which idiom did the friend use?
quests.hint: Once you've eaten the cake, it's gone - you can't still be holding it.
quests.explanation: 'You can't have your cake and eat it too' means you cannot enjoy two incompatible advantages at the same time — you must choose. Example: 'She wants both job security and total freedom — but you can't have your cake and eat it too.' It means something must be sacrificed.
options: have the best of both worlds
you can't have your cake and eat it too
kill two birds with one stone
make the most of every opportunity
quests.usageContext: Common as gentle, logical pushback when someone wants two things that can't both happen.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Social media lets businesses reach millions of customers instantly, but it also exposes them to public criticism that can spread uncontrollably. Which idiom captures this complexity?
quests.hint: A blade sharp on both sides can help you and cut you, depending on how it's used.
quests.explanation: 'A double-edged sword' means something that has both advantages and disadvantages at the same time. Example: 'Fame is a double-edged sword — you gain recognition but lose your privacy.' It comes from the image of a blade that cuts on both sides.
quests.usageContext: Common in balanced, thoughtful discussions weighing both advantages and disadvantages of something.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: Everything about the job offer was perfect, except that it required relocating to a city thousands of miles away from all her family and friends. Which idiom describes that single drawback?
quests.hint: Picture something small and unwanted spoiling an otherwise smooth, pleasant mixture.
quests.explanation: 'A fly in the ointment' means a minor flaw or problem that spoils an otherwise good situation or plan. Example: 'The hotel was beautiful, but the noisy road outside was a fly in the ointment.' It comes from a fly contaminating an otherwise perfect jar of ointment.
quests.usageContext: Common when pointing out one significant drawback within an otherwise appealing situation.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.

quests.question: The detective spent weeks suspecting the wrong person and pursuing entirely the wrong lead, wasting valuable time. Which idiom describes the detective's mistake?
quests.hint: Imagine a dog barking loudly up a tree where its target isn't actually hiding.
quests.explanation: 'Bark up the wrong tree' means to pursue a mistaken idea or look in the wrong place for something. Example: 'If you think I have the money, you're barking up the wrong tree.' It comes from hunting dogs that mistake which tree their prey has climbed.
quests.usageContext: Common when someone's reasonable-seeming theory or suspicion turns out to be mistaken.
quests.idiomOrigin: Dates back to Medieval European trade.
quests.visualMetaphor: Visualizing a hidden trap or obstacle.
